source: Podolak and Verma (2025) Read Your Own Mind: Reasoning Helps Surface Self-Confidence Signals in LLMs
finding: DeepSeek-R1-32B states confidence after its answer. With no reasoning it is barely better than chance. With a long forced chain of thought (budget forcing with 'Wait,'), its verbal confidence reaches the discrimination of semantic entropy from 10 samples. A separate reader model (GPT-4o-mini) sees only the trace and recovers the same signal.
numbers: 270 questions (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, MMLU, GSM8K, AIME24 mix after filtering). 100 to 500 reasoning tokens: accuracy 41% to 63%, verbal AUROC 0.56 to 0.80. Peak AUROC 0.88 vs near-random 0.56 at zero budget. Parity with semantic entropy at about 200 tokens on fact retrieval and about 3,500 tokens on maths; SE used 218 tokens per sample on average. At 3.4k tokens: R1 AUROC 0.851, reader 0.841, Spearman 0.57.
quote: test-time compute, not the particular uncertainty heuristic, is the decisive factor for obtaining reliable confidence estimates
limits: One model, 270 items (26 to 99 per sub-source, noisy), QA and short maths only, not multi-step agent work. Self-sampling hypothesis is inferred, not proven. Read from PDF text (pdftotext).
agent_relevance: Closes part of gaps 1 and 2. Confidence stated after reasoning is a summary of the trace, so it is worth using only after a real reasoning pass. At roughly equal tokens on fact retrieval, one long trace with a stated score matches k samples. Never ask for the number before or right after a no-reasoning answer.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence (Table 1 re-read)
finding: Table 1 now read row by row. Thinking-mode models have lower ECE than their non-thinking pair on TriviaQA in every backbone, though the EXAONE drop is small. Qwen3 is one checkpoint, so the difference comes from thinking, not from a different model. Reasoning models are better in 33 of 36 settings.
numbers: TriviaQA ECE (acc): Qwen3-32B non-thinking 0.207 (0.711) to thinking 0.063 (0.768); AUROC 0.650 to 0.807. Qwen2.5-32B-Inst 0.129 (0.718), R1-Distill-Qwen 0.042 (0.727), OR1-Preview 0.052, QwQ 0.063. GLM-4 0.084 to GLM-Z1 0.029. EXAONE-3.5 0.130 to EXAONE-Deep 0.104. NonambigQA Qwen3 ECE 0.403 to 0.226. In the table the Qwen3 Thinking row is identical to the QwQ row in every cell.
limits: Identical Qwen3 Thinking and QwQ rows look like a copy error; the Qwen3 numbers (0.207 to 0.063) are therefore not fully safe either. 32B open models only. No closed frontier models. Two-step prompt with forced confidence reasoning. Table rows read from the paper HTML via fetch tool and cross-checked against pdftotext cell values.
agent_relevance: Settles gap 7 in part. Direction is real and the Qwen2.5 pair (0.129 to 0.042) is confirmed. The Qwen3 pair is confirmed from the table but carries the duplicate-row doubt. Still no data on closed frontier models. Use thinking-mode confidence, and keep a per-model check.

source: Zeng, Xuan, Cui and Voigt (2025) Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
finding: Reasoning fine-tuning improves calibration on reasoning tasks but can worsen it on factual QA. Small open reasoning models answer far more often instead of saying 'I don't know'. RL reasoning models partly recover (a U-shape: instruct, then SFT reasoning worse, then RL better).
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME: accuracy 9.67% to 65.7%, ECE 0.752 to 0.240, AUROC 0.695 to 0.813. On SimpleQA and FreshQA small reasoning models are less calibrated than instruct models. Models state higher confidence with shorter reasoning.
limits: Open-source models of 14B to 32B, plus DeepSeek-R1. Factual part conflicts in direction with Yoon et al. d02; the difference is model set and task, not resolved. Read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: Competing result for gap 7. The thinking-improves-calibration effect holds on reasoning tasks (our case) and is not guaranteed on factual recall. Test on our own task mix before trusting any model-level claim.

source: Michael, BenShushan, Bien and Moore (2026) Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
finding: Preregistered study of 11 LLMs finds a hard-easy effect in LLMs: overconfidence is largest on hard question sets and models are underconfident on easy ones. The authors call regression to the mean the most parsimonious explanation but do not test it. Reasoning models show a much smaller hard-easy slope.
numbers: Models: 5 reasoning (R1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 and 3.7) and 6 chat. Sets: BoolQ 2503, SciQ 995, LSAT-AR 86, SAT-EN 173, HaluEval-QA 1790, LifeEval 751 items. Mean confidence 88% vs accuracy 79% (9 points over). Hard-easy coefficient: reasoning aggregate 0.168, chat aggregate 0.732 (range 0.192 to 0.996 by chat model). Reasoning ECE 0.037 vs chat 0.150. Correlation of confidence with correctness 0.94 vs 0.48. LifeEval hardest bin: confidence 34.2% vs actual 9.6%; easiest bin 80.5% vs 92.0%. 50.7% of LifeEval answers show no sign of table memorisation; 22.3% show strong memorisation (R1 71.5%).
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). No standard errors or tests for the coefficients. Item sets are not representative samples, difficulty is partly the benchmark's own; table counts disagree with the text for SAT-EN and LSAT-AR. Contamination is likely on LifeEval. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 answer: yes, the pattern appears in LLMs on six sets, but the study cannot tell effect from selection or noise artefact, so K03 stays contested. Reasoning models show a small slope (0.168), so a difficulty-dependent correction is low priority for a reasoning-model agent. Use a plain per-bin recalibration check on our own data instead.

source: Zhang, Xiong and Wu (2026) Agentic Confidence Calibration (Holistic Trajectory Calibration)
finding: In multi-step agents, verbalised end-of-run confidence is badly calibrated. A small calibrator trained on features of the whole trajectory (step dynamics, stability, position) improves ECE and AUROC. Positional features (late steps) are the most frequent first alert. Transfer to a new domain works only partly.
numbers: 8 benchmarks, 6 LLMs, smolagents and OAgents. Verbalised vs HTC-Reduced: SimpleQA ECE 0.121 vs 0.068, AUROC 0.655 vs 0.752; GPQA ECE 0.454 vs 0.102, AUROC 0.593 vs 0.706; HLE ECE 0.656 vs 0.031, AUROC 0.614 vs 0.644. About 500 trajectories per dataset (GAIA 165). MMLU-Pro to HLE transfer ECE 0.504. General calibrator on 7 pooled sets, zero-shot GAIA: ECE 0.118 (vs 0.142 direct-trained) but AUROC 0.647 vs 0.686.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Calibrator needs labelled trajectories and logprob/attention features, so it conflicts with our no-training rule in part (it is post-hoc, but needs model internals). Labels from a Gemini judge (90 to 95% human agreement). Small datasets. Learning curves only 100 to 400 samples.
agent_relevance: Gaps 5 and 9 partial: confidence from a whole run has weak discrimination (verbal AUROC 0.59 to 0.66); fixing ECE is cheap, fixing AUROC is not. Recalibration at several hundred labelled runs per domain is the scale seen. It does not transfer cleanly across domains, so recalibrate per task type.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Token-level confidence, taken locally (lowest group of tokens, or the tail of a trace), separates good and bad traces better than a whole-trace average, and lets a run stop early with no extra samples beyond a 16-trace warm-up. Aggressive filtering fails where confidence sits on a wrong answer.
numbers: Models: DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-8B and 32B, GPT-OSS-20B and 120B; AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25, GPQA-Diamond. AIME25 GPT-OSS-120B: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs majority vote 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. Online: low variant cuts tokens 43.8% to 84.7%; high variant 18.8% to 59.0%. Warm-up 8, 16, 32 give within 1 point. Top-10% filtering lowers accuracy in 8 of 20 offline settings by 0.31 to 4.69 points (GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 92.9% majority vs 88.9% to 90.5% filtered). No AUROC is reported for the confidence measures.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Needs top-k token logprobs. Maths and GPQA only. No equal-token head-to-head against one long trace; text and Table 2 disagree on the token-saving range (43 to 79% vs 84.7%).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: a local token-confidence dip is a cheap in-trace signal for stopping or re-examining, with no extra samples after warm-up. It is a fluency cue, so it fails on confident-wrong traces. Use it as a trigger, not a verdict, and pair with an outside check.

source: Kaddour et al. (2026) Agentic Uncertainty Reveals Agentic Overconfidence
finding: Coding agents asked to predict their own success on SWE-bench Pro are far overconfident and discriminate weakly. Asking before the work gives AUROC as good as or better than asking after it. Asking after, in an adversarial 'find the bugs' frame, lowers overconfident failures but costs about twice as much.
numbers: 100 SWE-bench Pro tasks; GPT-5.2-Codex, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5. True success 35%, 22%, 27%. Pre-execution predicted about 70%, 99%, 64%. AUROC pre/post/adversarial: GPT 0.62/0.58/0.55, Gemini 0.53/0.51/0.57, Claude 0.64/0.55/0.64. Pre vs post differences not significant (GPT CI 0.50 to 0.75 vs 0.46 to 0.70). Mid-run AUROC at 25/50/75% steps 0.49 to 0.64. Overconfident-failure rate 72% to 45% under adversarial review, steps 12.7 to 23.4, cost $0.23 to $0.52. Failing tasks predicted at 0.7 or more in 62% of cases vs passing tasks under 0.3 in 11%. Self-preference: GPT scored own patches +23 points (N=25).
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). One domain (coding), N=100, Gemini has 22 positives. Most pairwise differences not significant. Prompting only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9: post-run self-review did not beat pre-run guessing on discrimination, so stated confidence in a multi-step agent is a weak trigger (AUROC 0.5 to 0.65). Reviewing in an adversarial frame shifts calibration but costs double. Platt scaling alone fixed GPT ECE to 0.01 without helping AUROC, so use a cheap post-hoc map for calibration and an outside check for discrimination.

source: Barkan, Black and Sourbut (2025) Do Large Language Models Know What They Are Capable Of?
finding: All tested LLMs overestimate their success on coding tasks, most discriminate above chance. In multi-step tasks overconfidence of several models gets worse as the task goes on. Decisions follow the stated probability closely (near rational given that probability), so wrong confidence leads to wrong actions. Learning from in-context failures improves action mostly by accepting fewer tasks, not by discriminating better.
numbers: Exp 1: 1,140 BigCodeBench tasks. Exp 2: 512 sequences of 9 contracts (4,608 offers per model), $1 reward or penalty, 50% base rate; Sonnet 3.5 acceptance fell to about 50% by contract 5. Exp 3: 499 SWE-Bench Verified tasks, 10 models, 70 tool calls; all Sonnet models more overconfident by the end; only 4 of 10 models had after-the-fact AUROC above step 1; reasoning models no better. Decision classification accuracy near 1 given stated probability.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Exact AUROC and overconfidence values only in figures, not extracted. Coding tasks only. Reasoning budget zero in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 answer: yes, in these setups action follows stated confidence (threshold behaviour), so errors in confidence pass straight into action. That favours a threshold set from a recalibrated number, and a rule that never lets raw stated confidence alone decide. Multi-step runs get more overconfident with progress, so do not trust a late-step confidence more than an early one.

source: When Agents Disagree With Themselves: Behavioral Consistency as an Uncertainty Signal for LLM Agents (2026)
finding: For tool-using agents, how often repeated runs disagree in behaviour predicts failure much better than verbalised confidence. Majority vote adds almost nothing, but answering only when all runs agree raises accuracy at a cost in coverage. A fixed share of tasks are consistent and wrong.
numbers: HotpotQA 200 questions, 3 tools, k=10 at T=0.7 (8,000 runs); SWE-bench Verified 50 tasks, k=5. AUROC consistency vs verbalised (k=5): Claude Sonnet 4.5 0.651 vs 0.522; GPT-5 0.734 vs 0.547; Llama 70B 0.739 vs 0.481; combining did not beat consistency alone. Consistency AUROC range 0.62 to 0.78 at k=10. Majority-vote gain at k=3: Llama +2.0, Claude +0.7, GPT-5 +0.5, Gemini +0.1 points. Unanimous 3/3: 87.2% to 88.1% accuracy at 53.8% to 61.8% coverage (Gemini 73.4% at 64.7%). Consistent-wrong tasks: 5.5% to 10% of tasks.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Mainly HotpotQA with a 3-tool space; one annotator for consistent-wrong labels; about 30% of consistent-wrong Hard cases are fuzzy-match false negatives, so the Hard-stratum reversal is partly a scoring artefact. Observational. Equal-token comparison against one long trace not made (k runs cost k times).
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 4 and 9: in an agent loop, agreement of 3 to 5 runs beats verbalised confidence for deciding which tasks to verify (AUROC 0.65 to 0.74 vs 0.48 to 0.55) but costs k times as many tokens. About 5.5 to 10% of tasks remain confident and wrong, a floor that agreement cannot reduce. Use agreement only to route to a different-method check.

source: When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing Self-Consistency and Cross-Model Agreement as Confidence Signals (2026)
finding: Across GPT-4.1 tiers and a Claude check, self-consistency is only weakly related to majority correctness. A strong model can be highly consistent and wrong. Different model families share the same wrong answer more often than chance, so cross-model agreement does not remove it fully.
numbers: GPQA Diamond and AIME, 394 cases, 53 runners, K=50 samples (about 265,000). Spearman between consistency and correctness 0.20 to 0.59 over 12 cells (GPQA gpt-4.1 0.20, mini 0.30). gpt-4.1 mean consistency 0.89, majority accuracy 0.48 (mini 0.52); cases with consistency 0.8 or more wrong 48% (CI 0.40 to 0.56). Always-confidently-wrong: nano 0.09, mini 0.15, mini CoT 0.08, gpt-4.1 0.28; 50% of gpt-4.1 cases confidently wrong for at least one runner. gpt-4.1 ECE 0.41. Cross-family: same wrong answer on 10 of 15 shared wrong items for Haiku (p=.003), 10 of 14 Sonnet (p=.005), 6 of 12 Opus (p=.07). Early stop on consensus used about 60% fewer samples (19.8 vs 50). CoT raised accuracy +0.067 GPQA but barely raised the consistency-correctness link.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Mostly one provider; no reasoning models; runners wrote their own prompts; some GPQA items are ambiguous or mislabelled, inflating confident wrongness; snapshot dates not logged; small side studies (50 and 48 cases).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answer: confidently wrong and consistent is large (28% of GPQA items for the strongest tier, 8 to 15% for others). It is not fixed by more samples or a second model of another family (shared errors). It needs an outside check or a method that does not share the failure (a tool, a test, a different solving route). Supports K05 (reliability is not validity) with a second independent source.

source: Li et al. (2024) Few-Shot Recalibration of Language Models
finding: A global temperature fit hides slice-level miscalibration. A recalibrator that sees only k=20 unlabeled examples from the target slice tunes confidence per slice and beats global scaling and a labelled empirical map, including on unseen domains. It needs labelled data once to be trained.
numbers: PaLM2-L and LLaMA-65B/30B; MMLU 57 domains, XNLI 150 domains. ECE base, global temperature scaling, few-shot: MMLU PaLM2-L 0.063, 0.063, 0.053; XNLI 0.059, 0.057, 0.045; MMLU LLaMA-65B 0.109, 0.099, 0.074. Unseen XNLI domains ECE 0.049 vs 0.061 temperature scaling vs 0.064 base. k=5 already gives target-precision success 0.81. 20K synthetic training slices, 2K test slices.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Multiple-choice only, frozen base, 2023-era base models, training of a separate 7B recalibrator, so not allowed under our no-training rule. Paper has inconsistent step counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: the lesson, not the method. Per-slice calibration beats a single global map, and a few items per slice (5 to 20) carry useful information. Under our rule, use a per-task-type lookup table of observed accuracy by confidence bin, filled from our own graded runs, and expect the table to need many items per bin.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when all answers in a window agree. This keeps accuracy while saving most samples on easy items.
numbers: Window 5 (8 for MATH), max 40 (64 for MATH). Sample savings: GSM8K 80.1%, CommonsenseQA 78.5%, StrategyQA 76.8%, Coin Flip 84.2%, Last Letters 67.4%, MATH 33.8%. GPT-4 accuracy change 0.00 on MATH, GSM8K, CSQA. GPT-3.5 StrategyQA -0.19; LLaMA-2 7b StrategyQA -0.14 and Coin Flip -0.14. ESC vs full SC agreement 99.13% to 99.96%. False-positive stop bound 2e-3 at w=8, if the sample cap is infinite.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Older models; answers only (no agent tasks); savings smallest on hard MATH; accuracy loss sizeable for weaker models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial: agreement within the first few samples is a cheap stop-or-escalate trigger. Disagreement among two early samples is a conflict cue that costs only the extra sample, but the paper stops on unanimity of a window of 5 to 8, not 2.

source: Kossen et al. (2024) Semantic Entropy Probes
finding: A linear probe on one forward pass of hidden states predicts semantic entropy without sampling. It is weaker than true semantic entropy but generalises out of distribution better than a probe trained to predict accuracy.
numbers: Llama-2 7B/70B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3, Llama-3-70B; TriviaQA, SQuAD, BioASQ, NQ Open. Probe AUROC for capturing SE 0.7 to 0.95. In distribution SEP minus accuracy probe -2.0 to +2.8 points; out of distribution +2.2 to +10.5 points. 2,000 training pairs short-form, 1,000 long-form. Sampling SE costs 5 to 10 times.
limits: Read via fetch-tool extraction of the paper page, not the raw PDF (PDF download truncated). Needs hidden-state access and a trained probe, not available to a scaffold-only agent. Only linear probes. BioASQ results inflated by yes/no items.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: shows a one-pass uncertainty signal exists, but its form needs model internals. For our scaffold, the usable analogues are token logprobs (d06) and early-sample disagreement (d12), not hidden-state probes.

source: Finlay et al. (2026) CALIBER: Calibrating Confidence Before and After Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Argues confidence is state-dependent: before thinking it should predict whether the model will solve the prompt, after thinking whether this answer is right. Elicits both and trains each against a matching target.
numbers: 7B model on BigMathDigits: ECE down 52.5% relative to the best single-confidence baseline, with best Brier and AUROC, accuracy within 2.1 points. Out of distribution (GPQA, TriviaQA): best ECE and Brier. Separate pre- vs post-thinking AUROC not given on the page read.
limits: Abstract page only, no per-estimate table. Requires training. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no clean before vs after number found. The framing is useful: ask a 'can I solve this' question before work to budget effort and a separate 'is this answer right' question after work to gate checking. Do not mix them.

source: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review
finding: Delaying judgments of learning raises relative accuracy a lot and changes memory only slightly.
numbers: Meta-analysis 1: 4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes, gamma correlations, delayed vs immediate g = 0.93. Meta-analysis 2: 3,807 participants, 98 effect sizes, memory benefit g = 0.08.
limits: Abstract record only (via Europe PMC; full text paywalled; moderator tables not read). Learning of word pairs, not problem solving.
agent_relevance: Closes the number check in gap 8 (g=0.93 and 0.08 confirmed at abstract level). Transfer to LLMs not shown by this paper. See d17 for the cue condition that matters.

source: Kruger and Dunning (1999) Unskilled and unaware of it
finding: Bottom-quartile scorers on humour, grammar and logic tests grossly overestimated their performance. Training them raised their ability to see their limits.
numbers: 4 studies. Bottom quartile scored at the 12th percentile and estimated the 62nd.
limits: Abstract record only (Europe PMC); full text not read. Later work (Gignac, Dunkel; see K04) attributes much of the quartile pattern to statistics. Human, social and test-taking tasks.
agent_relevance: Confirms the headline number only. No LLM transfer. K04 stays: do not build a skill-dependent confidence correction on this pattern.

source: Dunlosky and Nelson (1992) Importance of the kind of cue for judgments of learning (JOL) and the delayed-JOL effect
finding: The delayed-JOL effect depends on the cue. It is very strong when the JOL cue is the stimulus alone and almost absent when the cue is the stimulus with its answer.
numbers: All 45 subjects showed the effect with a stimulus-only cue; little or no effect with a stimulus-response cue.
limits: Abstract record only (Europe PMC). Paired associates. Mechanism stated as unknown by the authors. The url is a Europe PMC search link, the record id was not captured.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 mapping: the LLM analogue of the delayed JOL is a fresh attempt from the question alone, not a re-read of question plus its own answer. Confidence judged while looking at the existing answer (the stimulus-response cue) is the weak form. Design the check as a blind re-solve, then compare.

source: Mind the Confidence Gap: Overconfidence, Calibration, and Distractor Effects in Large Language Models (2025)
finding: Across nine LLMs and three factual QA sets, large RLHF-tuned models can be more miscalibrated on easier queries. Adding distractors to the prompt reduced miscalibration.
numbers: 9 LLMs, 3 datasets. Distractors: ECE reductions up to 90%, relative accuracy gains up to 460%.
limits: Abstract page only. No human baseline. Prompt manipulation numbers are best cases.
agent_relevance: Weak support for gap 6: a difficulty-linked miscalibration (worse on easy) appears in chat models, consistent with d04. Not enough to build on.
